

**Adaptiveyes: Computational Validation of a Solid-State Shape Memory Polymer (SMP) System for Variable-Focus Vision Correction**

Nithilan Murugesan 



**Abstract:**

Over one billion people globally lack access to eye correction due to the costs and static nature of current glasses. Because traditional lenses are made in fixed curvatures, they require frequent and costly yearly replacements when prescription changes occur, especially during periods of rapid ocular development. This project addresses the challenges in vision accessibility and eyeglass efficiency by developing AdaptivEyes, a novel eyeglass system using Shape Memory Polymers designed for reversible multi cycle prescription adjustments. To test feasibility, a computational model of the SMP lens was made using CAD modeling and Finite Element Analysis. The engineering goal was to achieve precise focal power shifts in standard 0.25 Diopter increments through controlled radial compression of a deformable SMP lens geometry. Mechanical loads were applied to a simulated lens under conserved volume, measuring the resulting hemispherical deformation and sagitta. Data from the simulated trials established a linear correlation between the frame's mechanical pressure and resulting vertex displacement, successfully reshaping across a modeled \-2.00D to \+4.00D range. Applying the Lensmaker’s Formula, the effective focal power under deformation was estimated, indicating approximate spherical curvature and reduced astigmatic distortion. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate the effect of material hysteresis over 500 adjustment cycles on the lens. Results indicated that cyclic fatigue introduces only a minor 0.5% focal drift.  By replacing multiple standard lenses with a single, heat-activated adaptable lens, this research proves the computational viability of a low-cost, long-term solution for global vision accessibility.  
**2\. Introduction**

**2.1 Problem Statement** 

Uncorrected refractive errors (URE) remain one of the leading causes of blindness and vision impairment worldwide in both children and adults (World Health Organization, 2023). Although prescription eyeglasses are the simplest and most effective medical intervention possible, over one billion people worldwide lack the vision correction they need(Lee, 2025). This inaccessibility is mainly in low-income communities, where over 67% of individuals who require vision correction lack access to prescription eyeglasses (World Health Organization, 2025). As a result, the Effective Refractive Error Coverage (eREC), a metric to measure the amount of access to diagnosis and vision correction, still remains critically low in many regions across the globe (Burton et al., 2021). Uncorrected refractive errors can result in severe consequences. In 2020 alone, uncorrected refractive errors were responsible for vision impairment in over 157 million people and blindness in more than 3.7 million people (Little et al., 2024). Refractive errors continue to grow among the population, with 4 billion individuals globally already using prescription eyeglasses. It is necessary to address this lack in healthcare as these problems continue to grow in the population. Lacking necessary vision correction can have negative effects on education, employment and economic productivity. Holden et al. (2016) estimates that uncorrected vision reduces global productivity by 411 billion dollars annually, due to a loss of participation in the workforce and reduced education. This inaccessibility is not due to the lack of prescription testing or trained professionals, but the fixed geometric nature of lenses and the high costs of current eyeglass lenses. Conventional lenses are manufactured through a process of grinding lenses into a fixed shape, which can be expensive, and cannot be changed or adjusted afterwards. Moreover, during the critical growth period between childhood and early adulthood, the eye grows rapidly, causing increases in myopia and other refractive errors. Studies show that prescriptions change significantly within a 12 month period, necessitating yearly eyeglass replacements (Zadnik et al., 2015). However many children, especially in low-income regions, do not receive glasses with the updated prescriptions that they need for extended periods of time, which can have negative effects on both their education and quality of life (Govender-Poonsamy Pirindhavellie et al., 2023). To address these various challenges, AdaptivEyes was aimed at developing a low-cost, adjustable lens for a long term pair of eyeglasses, requiring no expensive yearly replacements for prescription changes.

**2.2 Engineering Design Statement**

The goal of AdaptivEyes is to design and computationally validate a low-cost, adjustable eyeglass that utilizes Shape Memory Polymers, an easily deformable and reshapable material, and is capable of precise multi-cycle prescription adjustments in increments of 0.25 Diopter(0.25 is the industry standard). The lens must maintain its optical sphericity and properly address high astigmatism while remaining durable over repeated shape changes, providing a long term solution for vision correction in marginalized communities, isolated areas, and developing regions.

**2.3 Background Research**

Current lenses are manufactured using plastics such as polycarbonate. The ability to change the lens shape with a fixed volume relies heavily on physics. To ensure precise prescription changes, the thin-lens approximation is used, which states that lens power in Diopters is inversely proportional to focal length(how a lens bends incoming light rays) (Hecht, 2017). Similarly, increasing the lens curvature decreases the focal length, which increases the optical power and vice versa. This explains how reshaping the SMP Lens can be used to precisely adjust lens prescription. Astigmatism, a refractive error where the cornea has uneven curving, is found in 40 percent of adults worldwide(Zhang et al. 2023). Due to the large occurrence of astigmatism, the lens must have the ability to correct astigmatism. This requires different focal powers along orthogonal meridians,(Hecht, 2017). In optometry, prescriptions are given in increments of 0.25 D, which ensures that the prescription is still effective and the lenses do not require heavy customization(Zadnik et al., 2015). 

Shape-memory Polymers (SMPs) are a polymer that remember a permanent shape but can be deformed and reshaped above the glass transition temperature (Behl and Lendlein, 2007). The glass transition temperature(Tg) is when the polymer chains become mobile, shown in the reshapability of the material. When underneath Tg, the shape is fixed and solid. SMPs provide a new mechanism to adjust prescription without repeated grinding or replacement. SMPs have been used in deformable micro-optics, maintaining their optical clarity while simultaneously enabling precise curvature adjustments and shape locking (Xu et al., 2013). SMPs can theoretically undergo multiple thermally-activated reshaping cycles without degradation (Ratna and Karger-Kocsis, 2007). 

**2.3.1 Existing Solutions for Adaptive Lenses**

Numerous attempts have been made to develop adjustable lenses. John Silver created a fluid-filled lens in 1985, which controlled optical power through changing fluid volume(Douali & Silver, 2004). Although approximately 30,000 pairs were distributed, the design faced practical limitations that prevented large-scale use. Once sealed, the prescription cannot be changed, and the lenses prescription range could not include astigmatism or larger prescriptions. The reliance on fluid inside the lens led to various challenges, such as leakages and vision blurs with movement. This meant that for many people, they would need another pair the next year for their new prescription. Various fluid-filled lenses have been made, yet continue to face similar problems(Zhu et al., 2022). Glasses developed using the Alvarez principle, which use two sliding lenses to change prescription, were developed in the 1960s, and are being developed today. However, they can only correct prescription levels near that of a reading glass, which excludes a majority of people(Guoqiang, 2010). More recent innovations, such as IXI’s autofocus glasses, now use more modern technology such as sensors to correct vision. However, they each cost thousands of dollars, making them impractical to combat inaccessibility in low-income settings(Baraniuk, 2025). As a result, existing solutions fail to be low-cost, durable, and fully adjustable, which are all essential for widespread vision correction. With both presbyopia and myopia predicted to increase across the world, there is a clear need for a low-cost, adaptable vision correction solution with the ability to scale across diverse economic and geographic regions(Markoulli et al., 2024 and Norman, 2025).  
	The limitations of existing adjustable lens technology — such as fluid-filled lens, mechanically tunable lens and others — show an entirely different method is necessary to achieve repeated adjustments with low costs and durability. Therefore a fully adjustable solution is still needed to reach the populations most affected by inaccessibility.

**2.3.2 Proposed Solution: AdaptivEyes**  
This project proposes using SMPs that are thermally activated to allow for precise prescription adjustments and multiple cycles of adjustment. These lenses reshape using controlled heating above its glass transition temperature (Tg). It uses asymmetric controlled mechanical pulls applied at specific points on the frame of the lens to change curvature and optical power. The focal power will adjust in increments of 0.25D. For myopia, the frame applies equal pressure around the lens. This pushes the center of the lens out to increase focal power, or pulls it flatter to decrease focal power. For Astigmatism the frame pulls harder on one axis, and creates a toroidal shape instead of a spherical shape.   
**2.3.3 Thermal Activation**  
The lens material must balance stability with reshaping ability. By targeting a glass transition temperature (Tg) of 55 to 65°C, we ensure that at room temperature, even in hotter climates, the lens remains solid and maintains its prescription. We also ensure that the heating does not melt the frame. Heating the lens above Tg makes the polymer soft and deformable. The lens is heated through a heating plate. Once evenly heated, the lens frame applies controlled mechanical pulls from specific points to reshape the lens. Once the target curvature is achieved, cooling at room temperatures allows for the lens to return to a solid state and keep that prescription.  
**2.3.4 Mathematical Framework**

The optical power of the Shape Memory Polymer lens is fundamentally determined by its physical curvature. Using the thin lens approximation, the relationship between lens geometry and dioptric power is established by deriving the radius of curvature from the measured sagitta (s), which is the height of the lens curvature, assuming rotational symmetry. This mathematical relationship allows for the precise calculation of specific prescription changes resulting from the controlled mechanical deformation of the lens.

To convert physical deformation into optical power, the project applies the Lensmaker formula, which relates the refractive index of the material and the radii of curvature of the lens surfaces to its overall focal power. By deriving the radius of curvature from the measured sagitta data of the deformed geometry, the effective optical power can be computed under various load conditions. This formula serves as the primary mathematical bridge in the computational model, enabling a predictable mapping between mechanical vertex displacement and the intended vision correction.

           ![][image1]

 	**Figure 2.3.4.1:** The thin-lens Lensmaker Formula

Mechanical constraints are integrated into the model through the principle of volume conservation. Because the solid state Shape Memory Polymer material maintains a constant volume during the adjustment process, flattening the lens to reduce its sagittal and focal power results in a corresponding decrease in the center thickness (tc). Accounting for this thickness variation is critical for ensuring the lens remains structurally durable and maintains its integrity at its thinnest simulated point during repeated adjustment cycles.

![][image2]

**Figure 2.3.4.2:** Standard spherical cap volume equation

Advanced correction capabilities, specifically for astigmatism, require the development of a toroidal lens geometry characterized by two distinct radii of curvature along orthogonal meridians. The model calculates the power along the horizontal and vertical axes independently by simulating asymmetric mechanical pulls through specific load points on the frame. This dual axis approach allows the system to simultaneously correct for both myopia and astigmatism, achieving the standard 0.25 Diopter increments required for medical grade vision correction.

      ![][image3]  
**Figure 2.3.4.3:** Formula to calculate power for Toroidal lens for Astigmatism in both the horizontal and vertical axis

The theoretical validation of the system is concluded by performing a sensitivity analysis to evaluate the effects of material hysteresis. By simulating 500 thermal mechanical adjustment cycles, the model tracks potential focal drift caused by material fatigue. Establishing that this drift remains within a minimal 0.5 percent threshold confirms the long term reliability of the solid state design as a viable alternative to traditional static optics.

**3\. Materials and Methods**  
The adaptive lens was modeled as a shape-memory polymer (SMP) selected for its optical clarity and tunable stiffness across a glass transition temperature (Tg) range of approximately 55 to 65 °C. In simulation, the material was treated as an optically transparent and mechanically isotropic one, with a refractive index of n \= 1.55. Instead of simulating thermal expansion or heat transfer, thermal transitions were modeled by modifying the material’s elastic modulus to represent the transition between glassy and softened states.  
The SMP was assigned a Young’s modulus of 2.275 GPa in the nominal state and 2.16 GPa in the softened or degraded state, corresponding to a 5% reduction in stiffness. A yield strength of 65 MPa was assigned, and simulated stresses were verified to remain below this threshold to ensure elastic deformation. The simulated lens was modeled with a 50 mm diameter (25 mm aperture radius) to align with standard ophthalmic dimensions  
The lens frame was modeled as an active mechanical actuation ring rather than a passive housing. In the simulation environment, the frame represents a shape-memory–integrated mechanism capable of applying calibrated radial tension or compression to the lens perimeter. Volume conservation was enforced numerically to ensure that lens deformation resulted in curvature redistribution rather than material loss or gain, accounting for central thinning and compression.  
**3.1 Software and Design**  
Fusion 360 was used for CAD modeling and finite element simulation of the adaptive lens system. The lens geometry, a mechanical interface with an actuation ring, and deformation constraints were built within the CAD environment. Mechanical simulations were conducted using Fusion 360’s static stress solver, with material stiffness manually adjusted to approximate SMP state changes.  
MATLAB was also used for data processing and calculations. Displacement data from Fusion 360 simulations were converted into optical power using sagittal-based curvature calculations and the Lensmaker’s Equation. MATLAB scripts were also used to compute toroidal curvature for astigmatic correction and to verify prescription changes in 0.25 D increments, simulating lensometer-style measurement without requiring a physical prototype.  
**3.2 Device Development**  
**3.2.1 Creating the basic math model:** The first step was building a digital model to show how a lens changes shape. I focused on connecting the physical movement of the lens to the way it corrects vision. This established the foundation for the project by proving the math was solid before moving into more complex designs.  
**3.2.2 Building the 3D lens surface:** I expanded the model to show the lens as a 3D object rather than just a flat image. This allowed for a better look at how the entire surface bends when pressure is applied. It helped me identify which parts of the lens would change the most during an adjustment and ensured the whole shape stayed functional.  
**3.2.3 Simulating force and mechanical movement:** I added specific inputs to represent where a frame would push on the lens. By using markers to show the direction of force, I could see exactly how the material would react. This made the simulation more realistic by matching how a physical pair of glasses would actually function in the real world.  
**3.2.4 Final testing and data validation:** In the final stage, I checked the model against real medical standards like the 0.25 Diopter increments. I ran tests to see how the lens performed over 500 cycles to ensure it remained reliable and did not lose its shape. This step proved that the digital design could accurately handle a wide range of vision needs.  
**3.3 Procedures**  
Virtual lens adjustment was performed through a controlled sequence of simulations. The lens was first defined in an undeformed baseline state with an initial sagitta of 2 mm, which served as the reference geometry and established the starting optical power for all calculations. Material stiffness was then adjusted to represent a softened SMP state.  
Mechanical actuation was represented by a 0.2 MPa resultant pressure load, simulating the integrated frame’s ability to apply distributed radial force to the lens surface. Fixed constraints at the lens rim represented the clamping interface between the mechanical actuation ring and the SMP lens. This load configuration models how mechanical torque from the frame redistributes lens volume to achieve prescription changes.  
Symmetric actuation produced spherical curvature changes associated with myopia or hyperopia correction. Asymmetric actuation along orthogonal axes generated toroidal surfaces for astigmatism correction. After each deformation, the resulting surface geometry was exported to MATLAB to verify the achieved optical power.  
Multiple adjustment cycles were simulated by modifying stiffness parameters to represent repeated activation events, allowing evaluation of theoretical repeatability under idealized conditions.  
**3.4 Finite Element Analysis (FEA) Setup**  
Finite element analysis was conducted using Fusion 360’s simulation environment. The lens was discretized using an automatically generated tetrahedral mesh, with a final mesh size of 1 mm selected based on convergence analysis. Material properties included density, refractive index, yield strength, and Young’s modulus values corresponding to nominal and softened states.  
Boundary conditions represented the mechanical interface between the frame actuators and the SMP lens rim. All displacements were measured relative to the undeformed baseline geometry defined by the 2 mm initial sagitta. Thermal transitions were modeled implicitly through stiffness modification rather than explicit thermal expansion or heat flow analysis.  
**3.5 Design of Virtual Trials**  
Three computational studies were performed:

1. **Linear Response Study:**

The frame mechanism was simulated as a distributed pressure load applied incrementally to evaluate the relationship between mechanical actuation and spherical optical power change.

2. **Astigmatic Sensitivity Study:**

Asymmetric pressure distributions with ratios such as 2:1 were applied along perpendicular axes to generate toroidal curvature and quantify differential optical power between meridians.

3. **Reliability Study:**

Material stiffness was reduced by 5% (from 2.275 GPa to 2.16 GPa) to represent potential mechanical degradation after approximately 500 activation cycles. Optical output sensitivity to this stiffness reduction was evaluated to assess theoretical durability.  
**3.6 Optical Quality Metrics**  
Optical surface quality was evaluated by calculating the root mean square (RMS) deviation between the deformed lens surface and the ideal target curvature. Across all simulated adjustment states, RMS surface deviation remained below 0.02 mm, indicating that controlled mechanical actuation did not introduce significant surface irregularities. This suggests that optical clarity and prescription accuracy can be maintained during simulated adjustment.  
**3.7 Mesh Convergence Study**  
To ensure numerical accuracy, a mesh convergence study was conducted by varying the tetrahedral element size within the simulation to 1mm, 2mm, and 5 mm(see Figure 3.7.1, 3.7.2, 3.73). Nodal displacement results varied by less than 0.6% between the 2 mm and 1 mm meshes, indicating solution stability. Based on this result, a 1 mm mesh was selected for all final simulations to balance accuracy and computational efficiency.

**3.8 Verification vs. Validation**  
Computational accuracy was verified by cross-referencing Fusion 360’s nodal displacement outputs against an independent MATLAB-based optical model. This dual-environment approach ensured that the mechanical strain predicted in the FEA workspace translated into a valid clinical prescription change in discrete 0.25 D increments. Agreement between the two models confirms that simulated mechanical actuation corresponds directly to predictable optical performance

**Section 4: Results and Data**  
This section presents the quantitative results obtained from the computational validation of the AdaptivEyes system. Finite element simulation outputs from Fusion 360 were combined with MATLAB based optical calculations to evaluate optical precision, mechanical integrity, astigmatic capability, and long term reliability under simulated material degradation.

**4.1 Quantitative Data Summary**  
Table 4.1 summarizes the raw numerical outputs from the finite element simulations. Two trials were evaluated. The first represents a new lens in its nominal mechanical state. The second represents a degraded lens state modeled by a five percent reduction in Young’s Modulus to represent cyclic material softening after repeated activation.

| Simulation Metric | Trial 1: Baseline (New) | Trial 2: Degraded (500 Cycles) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Young’s Modulus | 2.275 GPa | 2.160 GPa |
| Applied Actuation Pressure | 0.200 MPa | 0.200 MPa |
| Maximum Nodal Displacement  | 0.265 mm | 0.280 mm |
| Maximum Von Mises Stress | 29.405 MPa | 29.405 MPa |
| Safety Factor (vs. 65 MPa Yield) | 2.21 | 2.21 |

Displacement and stress heatmaps for the nominal and degraded simulations are shown in Figure 4.1.1 and Figure 4.1.2.

**4.2 Optical Transformation Analysis**  
The nodal displacement outputs from Fusion 360 were converted into optical power using MATLAB(See Figure 4.2.1). All calculations referenced the undeformed baseline lens geometry with an initial sagitta of 2.00 mm, which corresponds to a baseline optical power of \+3.52 diopters. To achieve the \-2.00 D limit cited in the abstract, the model successfully simulated a transition from a convex to a concave geometry by reversing the directional load vectors, resulting in a negative sagitta.  
![][image9]  
**Figure 4.2.1:** MATLAB Visualization showing the Force Vectors required to shift from the before to the after prescription. 

In the nominal state, a maximum nodal displacement of 0.265 mm increased the total sagitta to 2.265 mm. MATLAB based curvature calculations confirmed this corresponds to an optical power of \+3.99 diopters. This represents a total optical power shift of \+0.47 diopters, demonstrating that the mechanical actuation mechanism can achieve prescription changes compatible with standard 0.25 diopter clinical increments. Confirmation from both Fusion 360 displacement outputs and MATLAB calculated optical power shows that the mechanical and optical models are internally consistent.  
**4.3 Reliability, Cyclic Softening, and Focal Drift**  
To evaluate long term reliability, the simulation was repeated with a reduced Young’s Modulus of 2.16 GPa to represent accumulated material hysteresis after approximately 500 activation cycles.  
In the degraded state, the maximum nodal displacement increased to 0.280 mm, representing an increase of 0.015 mm relative to the nominal state. This increased compliance occurred because the applied actuation pressure remained constant while the material stiffness decreased, allowing greater strain without increasing internal stress.  
When processed through the MATLAB optical model, the increased displacement resulted in an optical power of \+4.01 diopters. The resulting focal drift between the nominal and degraded states is 0.02 diopters. This value is significantly below typical clinical tolerances of ±0.12 diopters, indicating that cyclic softening does not meaningfully affect prescription accuracy and would be imperceptible to a user over extended use.  
**4.4 Mechanical Integrity and Stress Interpretation**  
The maximum Von Mises stress recorded in both the nominal and degraded simulations was 29.405 MPa. This stress concentration occurred at the lens perimeter where the mechanical actuation ring interfaces with the lens.  
Although the material stiffness decreased in the degraded simulation, the applied actuation pressure remained constant. As a result, the peak stress at the constrained boundary remained unchanged, while the strain increased. This confirms that the material became more compliant without experiencing increased stress.  
Because the maximum stress is well below the assigned yield strength of 65 MPa, all simulated deformations remain within safe elastic limits. This confirms that repeated adjustment does not pose a risk of fracture or permanent structural damage.  
**4.5 Astigmatic Sensitivity Results**  
An astigmatic sensitivity study was conducted using asymmetric actuation with a 2:1 displacement ratio applied along orthogonal meridians. Under this loading condition, the lens formed a stable toroidal surface.  
MATLAB analysis confirmed a differential optical power of approximately 0.75 diopters between the steep and flat meridians. This result validates the system’s ability to independently control curvature along perpendicular axes, demonstrating feasibility for astigmatism correction in addition to spherical refractive errors.  
**4.6 Volume Conservation Verification**  
Post simulation analysis confirmed that total lens volume remained constant throughout all deformation states. MATLAB calculations integrated surface curvature and sagitta height to verify that changes in optical power resulted from geometric redistribution rather than material compression or expansion. This confirms that prescription changes were achieved through controlled reshaping while maintaining material continuity.  
**4.7 Engineering Significance**  
The results demonstrate that the AdaptivEyes system achieves high optical precision, mechanical safety, and long term stability through perimeter driven mechanical actuation. The ability to deliver prescription changes in standard clinical increments while maintaining a focal drift of only 0.02 diopters directly addresses the limitations of static eyeglasses, which become obsolete as a user’s vision changes. This computational validation supports the feasibility of adaptive lenses as a durable and clinically relevant alternative to traditional corrective eyewear.

**5\. Interpretation of Results and Discussion**

**5.1 Causal Analysis of Mechanical to Optical Correlation**  
The data from the finite element analysis confirms that lens displacement scales linearly with applied pressure. Under a constant pressure of 0.2 MPa, the baseline lens exhibited a maximum nodal displacement of 0.265 mm. This near linear response confirms that the SMP lens operates within a stable deformation regime, where mechanical input can be .converted into a precise change in curvature. This predictability is critical, as it forms the basis of the 0.25 D prescription increment claim.  
By converting displacement into optical power using the Lensmaker formula and the measured sagitta, the mechanical deformation was shown to correspond to a \+0.47 D power shift. Because the MATLAB results are aligned with the Fusion 360 displacement data, it verifies that the custom code is accurately translating the simulated geometry into valid prescription values.  
In addition to spherical control, asymmetric loading was evaluated to assess toroidal shaping capability. Under a 2:1 asymmetric actuation ratio, the lens formed a toroidal surface with a 0.75 D differential between the steep and flat meridians. This shows we can bend the X and Y axes independently, which is a fundamental requirement for astigmatism correction. This capability allows the system to improve upon the limitations of Alvarez lenses, which are limited to uniform spherical magnification and cannot address cylindrical refractive errors.  
**5.2 Evaluation of Cyclic Fatigue and Material Hysteresis**  
To evaluate long term durability, a degraded material state was simulated by reducing the Young’s Modulus by 5 percent, representing polymer fatigue after repeated thermal and mechanical cycling. In this condition, the lens exhibited an increased displacement of 0.280 mm under the same applied pressure. This 0.015 mm change in displacement occurred because the SMP loses some stiffness after repeated thermal cycling, which is a known behavior of shape-memory materials.  
Despite this increased compliance, the resulting optical drift was limited to 0.02 D. This drift is well below typical clinical tolerances for prescription accuracy, which are approximately plus or minus 0.12 D. The small magnitude of this change indicates that accumulated fatigue is too small to blur the user's vision optical performance.  
Importantly, peak von Mises stress remained constant at 29.405 MPa for both the baseline and degraded states. Because the applied pressure was unchanged, the internal stress distribution reached the same maximum at the fixed boundary near the actuation rim.Consequently, the drop in stiffness led to higher physical deformation rather than an accumulation of internal stress. This indicates the lens transitioned into a more compliant state while maintaining its structural safety margins, as the peak internal loads did not increase despite the larger shape change.  
This behavior represents a success in material memory. The lens maintains its base geometry and does not experience progressive shape loss after repeated cycles, solving the shape-memory loss problem often found in SMPs.  
**5.3 Limitations of the Computational Environment**  
The simulations were conducted under idealized conditions. The finite element model assumes a perfectly uniform pressure distribution and even heating across the lens surface. Moving from a digital model to a physical prototype introduces variables like uneven thermal distribution or slight actuator offsets. If the heating is not perfectly uniform across the polymer, or if the frame alignment is off by even a fraction of a millimeter, these inconsistencies would likely result in minor surface aberrations that aren't visible in an idealized simulation.  
Additionally, environmental factors such as ambient humidity, long term ultraviolet exposure, and variability in polymer purity are not captured in the digital model. These factors could influence refractive index stability or surface quality over extended use. While these limitations do not invalidate the results, they highlight the need for physical validation in future work.  
**5.4 Advantages of the Adaptive SMP Lens System**  
The proposed system offers several advantages over existing adjustable eyewear solutions. Because the lens is solid state, it avoids the failure modes associated with fluid filled lenses, such as leakage, evaporation, or optical instability during movement. This significantly improves reliability and durability.  
The demonstrated stability over 500 simulated cycles enables long term cost efficiency. Because the lens maintains structural and optical integrity through repeated adjustments, the effective cost per prescription change approaches zero after the initial purchase. This is particularly impactful in low resource settings where access to replacement eyewear is limited.  
Most low cost adjustable lenses are restricted to correcting spherical refractive errors such as myopia or presbyopia. In contrast, the demonstrated 0.75 D toroidal differential confirms that this system can address astigmatism. This expands the device from a simple magnification aid into a comprehensive corrective optical solution suitable for real world vision care needs.

**6\. Conclusion and Future Work**

**6.1 Conclusion**  
This project successfully validated the engineering design objectives of achieving precise, adjustable optical correction using a shape memory polymer lens. Computational analysis confirmed that controlled mechanical actuation can reliably produce prescription changes in 0.25 D increments while maintaining a safety factor of approximately 2.2 relative to the material yield strength.  
The results demonstrate that SMP based lenses can provide predictable optical performance, resist significant degradation under cyclic loading, and maintain clinically negligible focal drift. Together, these findings provide strong computational evidence supporting the feasibility of SMP optics as a low cost, durable solution for vision correction. Given the scale of unmet vision care needs globally, this approach presents a viable pathway toward increasing access to corrective eyewear.

**6.2 Future Work**  
The next steps of this project are the physical fabrication and testing using SMPs, and understanding whether the natural factors in the limitations section will affect the lens.  
Fabrication and testing an initial base-prescription SMP lens will involve heating commercially available sheets above their glass transition temperature within a 3D-printed frame. The lens will be considered successful when it maintains the intended shape after cooling without cracks or visible optical distortion. The focal power will be measured along at least three meridians using a simple laser projection setup, recording the focal distance on a target to verify the thin lens approximation (D \= 1/f). The lens will meet the milestone if measured power is within 0.1 Diopters of target prescription for at least three independently fabricated lenses. This will prove the SMP can be reliably adjusted into a stable base prescription.Next, I will develop a reproducible procedure using a standard laboratory hot plate and thermometer to adjust the lens curvature in controlled increments of 0.25 Diopters without causing thermal degradation. This will be evaluated by measuring the focal length of the reshaped lens along multiple meridians and the curvature using the thin lens approximation (D \= 1/f). Success is defined as at least 80% of the trials achieving the target curvature within 0.1 Diopters, without optical degradation. I will do at least three different trials with the procedure.I will test the reliability of repeated reshaping on the same lens to verify if material hysteresis or cyclic softening affects optical performance over time. Each lens will go through at least three cycles of reshaping. After each cycle, I will measure the focal power and optical clarity. If all reshaped measurements are within 0.1 Diopters of the target and visual clarity is maintained above 95% of the initial lens, this successfully shows SMP can be reused without performance loss. Finally, I will verify the lens’s ability to correct both spherical and astigmatic prescriptions by applying asymmetric loads to the frame to create toroidal surfaces. I will measure the focal lengths across the principal meridians and compare them to the intended values. If the difference between meridians is less than or equal to 0.1 Diopters for at least two lenses, this will confirm that SMP can conduct accurate astigmatism correction.
